findings.claim: The 'first post-retrieval quality estimation framework purpose-built for multilingual agent skills' claim (lines 117-119) is accurate as worded, but its novelty rests entirely on the 'quality estimation (vs relevance)' and 'multilingual' qualifiers: post-retrieval LLM-based selection over agent-skill candidates already exists in the cited SkillFlow baseline that the paper reimplements, so the framework class is not new — reviewers should size the methodological contribution as those two qualifiers plus the constructed benchmark, which the paper itself declares.
findings.why_it_matters: The conjunction of four qualifiers is doing all the work in the headline novelty sentence. This is not a false claim, but reviewers and readers should weigh it as 'first to combine known pieces in a partly self-constructed setting' rather than 'first to conceive post-retrieval skill judgment' - the latter reading is invited by the surrounding prose but not supported.
findings.verifier_note: The quotes and the external SkillFlow verification hold, and the qualifier analysis is accurate: the 'first' claim (lines 117-119) is protected by 'quality estimation' and 'multilingual', and post-retrieval LLM selection over agent skills pre-exists in SkillFlow — which the paper openly acknowledges by reimplementing it (lines 475-478) and running its ranking stage as a baseline (lines 494-496), so nothing is hidden. But the finding's sharpest clause overreaches: 'the multilingual agent skills setting barely exists in the wild (Table 1: sw/hi at 0)' cherry-picks the two zero-count languages from a table that also shows roughly 5,000 genuine non-English in-language skill bodies (zh ~4,000, fr ~700, ko ~200, ja ~80, lines 51-54); the Tool Use tasks come from a published 52-language function-calling benchmark (Kulkarni et al. 2025, lines 393-396); and the self-constructed pools are declared, motivated as mirroring the practical MT+self-generation layering (Sec 5.2 lines 429-435), and released as a claimed contribution (lines 125-127). A rebuttal citing these facts defeats the insinuation that the setting is an artifact of the paper's own construction, leaving only the (accurate, self-conceded) observation about where the novelty load sits.

findings.title: Positioning overstates the data-quality line as judging 'only the data's own language quality', contradicting the paper's own description of DEITA two sentences earlier
findings.evidence: Line 196-197: "quality scorers such as DEITA (Liu et al. 2024) likewise select instruction data on intrinsic quality alone." Then line 197-199: "These pipelines judge only the data's own language quality, leaving out skill-use dimensions such as executability and context efficiency." And in the positioning paragraph: "The data-quality line, in turn, stops at the data's own language quality."
findings.claim: DEITA scores general instruction complexity and quality (an English-language, LLM-scored notion of intrinsic data quality), not 'language quality'; JQL scores multilingual pretraining-document quality in an education-value style. Reducing the whole line to 'language quality' is inaccurate for at least DEITA, and the paper's own earlier sentence ('intrinsic quality alone') is the correct characterization.
findings.why_it_matters: The operative contrast (static intrinsic quality vs execution-grounded, query-conditioned utility) is fair and survives; but the 'only language quality' wording paints the compared line as narrower than it is, which slightly pads M-SQE's claimed gap. A one-sentence rewording fixes it; as submitted it is an unfair characterization of a cited baseline family.
findings.verifier_note: I tried to refute this and could not. Quotes verified exactly: line 196-197 'quality scorers such as DEITA (Liu et al. 2024) likewise select instruction data on intrinsic quality alone' (accurate), then lines 197-199 'These pipelines judge only the data's own language quality' and lines 205-206 'The data-quality line, in turn, stops at the data's own language quality' (inaccurate for DEITA, which scores complexity and quality of English instruction/response data via LLM scoring — not linguistic/language quality in the sense this multilingual paper otherwise uses, i.e., translationese, mistranslation, localization, cf. lines 96-98 and dimensions 4-5 at lines 239-241). The charitable rebuttal ('language quality' = 'quality of the data as language material') concedes a rephrase to the paper's own correct wording one sentence earlier, which is precisely what the finding asserts. The finding is correctly self-limited: it does not claim the positioning gap (no executability/context-efficiency dimension in that line) is wrong — that gap holds for DEITA and JQL regardless — so it survives rebuttal as a precise minor wording defect.

findings.title: The verified-skill-synthesis line (SkillGen, CoEvoSkills) is cited but excluded from the positioning, and the citation bundle presenting them as multilingual synthesis misfits their scope
findings.location: Sec 1 (p2, lines 86-88); Sec 3 'Positioning M-SQE' (p3, lines 200-210); Sec 5.2 (p5, lines 450-453); References (SkillGen 'Verified Inference-Time Agent Skill Synthesis'; CoEvoSkills 'Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Co-Evolutionary Verification')
findings.evidence: Sec 1: "A practical way to close this gap is to synthesize more multilingual skills (Long et al. 2024; Ma et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2026)" - yet by their cited titles, Ma et al. 2026 (SkillGen: 'Verified Inference-Time Agent Skill Synthesis') and Wang et al. 2026 (SkillX: 'Automatically Constructing Skill Knowledge Bases for Agents') are general skill-synthesis works, and Long et al. 2024 is a synthetic-data survey; none is multilingual synthesis. Sec 3's positioning claims the skill-retrieval line "asks neither whether a matched skill is intrinsically sound, nor whether the skill will actually work for the task at hand" and names only two prior lines, while the paper's own description of Voyager in the same section says its "skill library lets an agent accumulate and reuse verified action sequences."
findings.claim: Sec 3's two-gap positioning (lines 200-206) omits a third line the paper itself cites — creation-time skill verification (Voyager's verified library, SkillGen, CoEvoSkills) — and never engages whether verified synthesis would shrink the Theory view's intrinsic-quality niche (the Action view's query-grounded role is safe by construction, and Sec 1 lines 88-98 already argues unverified MT/self-generation is unstable); additionally, the citations attached to 'synthesize more multilingual skills' (lines 86-88) are general synthesis works and a survey, none multilingual — a minor positioning and citation-precision gap.
findings.why_it_matters: Generate-and-verify is the most natural competing paradigm to retrieve-then-score: if pool skills arrived verified, much of the Theory view's job would be done upstream. The positioning would be strengthened, not weakened, by engaging this line explicitly; as written, the two-gap story is achieved partly by leaving the third line out, and the Sec 1 bundle mislabels two of these works as multilingual synthesis.
findings.verifier_note: Partly verified, partly wrong on location. Verified: Sec 3's positioning names exactly two lines ('The two lines above leave complementary gaps... M-SQE fills both', lines 200-206) and does not engage creation-time verification, despite the paper citing Voyager's 'verified action sequences' (lines 169-170), SkillGen ('Verified Inference-Time Agent Skill Synthesis', lines 852-855), and CoEvoSkills ('Co-Evolutionary Verification', lines 892-895); and the Sec 1 citation triple for 'synthesize more multilingual skills' (lines 86-88) is, by the cited works' own titles, general synthesis work plus a synthetic-data survey, none multilingual. But the claim 'the paper never argues why creation-time verification does not shrink the niche... its implicit answer is in Sec 5.2, not in the positioning' misreads the paper: the argument appears in the introduction immediately after the synthesis citation — lines 88-98 argue that MT and self-generation 'neither is stable in quality', citing Li et al. 2026 (self-generated skills can hurt) and Liu et al. 2026c (MT content errors) — and the positioning paragraph itself claims the Action view measures 'how much a specific skill will help the query at hand' (lines 208-210), which no creation-time verifier can supply. So the niche defense exists for realistic unverified pools and for the Action view; what the paper genuinely never addresses is the narrower Theory-view overlap: whether verified synthesis (SkillGen-style), if adopted, would obviate selection-time intrinsic-quality certification.

findings.title: Citation practice: two references never cited in the main text, thin support for a 'widely adopted' claim, and several load-bearing roles filled from one overlapping-author cluster
findings.location: References p8 (Hu et al. 2022 LoRA, lines 769-772; Karpukhin et al. 2020 DPR, lines 779-783); Sec 5.4 (p6, lines 576-579); Secs 4.2, 5.3 (taxonomy and baselines)
findings.evidence: Grep of the full provided text: Karpukhin et al. 2020 and Hu et al. 2022 appear only in the reference list, never in the body (presumably used in supplementary Appendix F, which I cannot see). Sec 5.4: Gemini-3-Flash is "chosen for its balance of multilingual quality and speed, a trade-off widely adopted in recent multilingual agent research (Liu et al. 2026a,b)" - the sole support for 'widely adopted' is two papers (MADE, GaoYao) whose author lists heavily overlap with each other and with MIDB (Liu et al. 2026c) and M-DaQ (Zhao et al. 2026). Counting the 36 references: roughly 15-16 receive substantive individual treatment (a specific claim, role, or reimplementation attached); the rest are bundled cites, dataset/repo pointers (LittleDinoC, wshobson, huzey; six culture datasets), or unanchored; 9 of 36 are 2026 arXiv preprints (normal for this field, noted, not itself a defect).
findings.claim: One overlapping-author research cluster (MIDB, M-DaQ, MADE, GaoYao, CultureScope, SAGE — 6 of 36 refs) supplies the Theory-view taxonomy's cited inspiration, one of the three quality-scorer baselines, two of the six culture task sources, and the only citations behind the 'trade-off widely adopted in recent multilingual agent research' claim (line 579), which should either cite independent work or be softened — though the backbone choice itself is separately supported by the Fig. 6 robustness sweep; separately, Hu et al. 2022 and Karpukhin et al. 2020 are uncited in the provided main text and their usage (presumably Appendix F) is unverifiable from the provided material.
findings.why_it_matters: None of this is misconduct and the key external premises verified accurate (see strengths). But 'widely adopted' resting on a two-paper same-cluster bundle is weak support for a design decision, and the concentration of taxonomy, baseline, and backbone justification in one line means the paper's framing of the multilingual-quality literature is narrower than the field; the orphan references should be anchored or moved to the supplementary bibliography.
findings.verifier_note: I re-ran the grep myself: 'Hu et al.'/'LoRA' and 'Karpukhin'/'Dense Passage' appear only in the reference list (lines 769-772, 779-783), never in the provided body — the orphan observation is factually correct. But under this review's process rules the 'hygiene gap' framing does not survive: the paper defers 'all other implementation details' to Appendix F (line 569) in unprovided supplementary material, and both references have obvious appendix roles (LoRA for Table 5's Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning, lines 712-714/727-728; DPR for the dense retriever), so the correct status is 'unverifiable from the provided material', not a defect — the finding itself half-concedes this ('presumably used in supplementary Appendix F'). The cluster facts verify fully: MIDB, M-DaQ, MADE, GaoYao, CultureScope, and SAGE (6 of 36 refs) share overlapping author sets (Tao S., He M., et al. appear across all six), and they supply the Theory-view taxonomy inspiration (line 244), one of three quality-scorer baselines (line 559), two of six culture sources (lines 418-421), and the sole support for 'widely adopted' (line 579). But 'the entire justification for the scorer/solver backbone choice' overstates: Fig. 6 (lines 670-706) empirically varies scorer and solver backbones and shows +3.5-9.0pp gains across all six configurations, so the backbone choice has independent empirical support — only the 'widely adopted' breadth claim rests on the two in-cluster citations. Also, the taxonomy is claimed to be 'further extended' by an expert team (lines 244-248, deferred to Appendix D, unverifiable), so it is not solely cluster-derived.

findings.title: Abstract's 'at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers' does not hold per retriever; recomputed deltas over the strongest baseline are +4.5, +3.1, +3.0

findings.claim: The abstract sentence 'exceeds existing baseline's average by at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers' (lines 24-26) is ambiguously worded: under a per-retriever reading against the strongest baseline it is false for two of three retrievers (+3.07 Neural, +2.97 SkillFlow, vs +4.50 BM25, recomputed from Table 3), and it holds only as the pooled nine-setting margin (+3.51, 69.1 vs 65.6); the abstract should adopt Sec 5.5's unambiguous phrasing ('+3.5pp over the strongest baseline, SkillFlow, on the nine-setting average').
findings.why_it_matters: This is the headline superiority number in the abstract, phrased to imply per-retriever robustness at a margin the table does not support. It is a small, precise wording defect - easily fixed by 'a +3.5-point average across nine retriever-domain settings' - but as written it overstates the contribution bullet the novelty claim leans on.
findings.verifier_note: All arithmetic reproduces exactly from Table 3: M-SQE per-retriever three-domain averages 68.17 (BM25) / 68.80 (Neural) / 70.40 (SkillFlow); strongest per-retriever baseline (SkillFlow selector) 63.67 / 65.73 / 67.43; deltas +4.50 / +3.07 / +2.97; pooled nine-setting 69.12 vs 65.61 = +3.51. However, three points blunt the finding as stated. (1) The 'natural reading' assertion is contestable: 'exceeds existing baseline's average by at least +3.5 points across three different retrievers' uses a singular 'baseline's average', and 'across three different retrievers' plausibly scopes the average (computed across all three retrievers) rather than quantifying per-retriever — a per-retriever claim would say 'for each retriever'. (2) Under the pooled reading the margin is 3.51, so 'at least +3.5' is literally true, not merely 'exactly' as the finding rhetorically puts it. (3) The finding's 'true only under the pooled-average reading' is incomplete: under the reading 'the average of existing baselines' (the six external baselines average 58.0 pooled; per-retriever margins are +12 to +13pp), the sentence is true and massively understated. What survives is an ambiguity defect — the abstract admits a stronger reading that is false — not a demonstrated overstatement.

findings.title: Contested cultural norms are encoded as single deterministic gold answers, under an unjustified six-region taxonomy that lumps 'Africa and the Middle East'
findings.evidence: "Task types span etiquette, gift-giving, and dining customs"; "A response counts as correct only when it matches the checker's target exactly — a gold string or accepted paraphrase"; "a self-generated Lunar New Year skill can name the right occasion and still misstate the customary amount"; "six cultural regions worldwide (East and Southeast Asia, South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Middle East, the Americas, and Oceania)"
findings.claim: Deterministic single-target checking is applied to norm-type cultural tasks (etiquette, gift-giving, dining customs) whose correct answers plausibly vary within a region — the paper's own Sec 4.4 example treats 'the customary amount' for Lunar New Year red envelopes as a single recoverable fact — and the six-region scheme collapses 'Africa and the Middle East' and 'the Americas' into single buckets with no main-text justification or acknowledgment of intra-region variation. Whether Appendix D/G's gold selection and paraphrase-acceptance sets accommodate legitimate variation, and whether the Sec 5.1 verifiability filter reliably excludes contested norms, is unverifiable from the provided material. This is a debatable design choice requiring author clarification (show how regionally variant norms were handled), not a demonstrated error.
findings.why_it_matters: A framework whose stated purpose is 'advancing cultural equality' risks reproducing the flattening it targets: it rewards agents for asserting one norm per culture point. This is a design choice a rebuttal can defend (source benchmarks like NormAd do similar), but the paper never surfaces or defends it, which for an equality-framed submission is a substantive ethics gap in the reviewed material.
findings.verifier_note: All four quotes verify (Sec 5.1 lines 421-427; Sec 5.4 lines 563-566; Sec 4.4 lines 349-351; region list lines 421-423), and no main-text sentence acknowledges intra-region variation or justifies the six-bucket scheme. But the strong 'essentialism' form is blunted by three things the finding under-weighs: (1) Sec 5.1's stage-1 filter keeps 'only tasks whose success a deterministic checker can decide' — decidability is a stated, deliberate inclusion criterion, not an oversight, so tasks with genuinely contested answers are claimed to be filtered out; (2) the checker accepts 'a gold string or accepted paraphrase', and whether acceptance sets encode legitimate variant norms is precisely the Appendix G content that cannot be seen — 'one checker-decidable correct answer' asserts what is actually unverifiable; (3) each task is 'derived from a culture point' in six named published culture resources, which answers 'whose norm' at the resource level even though the specific mapping is unprovided.

findings.title: Sec 2's region-level equality evidence rests on ~9-15 tasks per region; the cited 'strong gains' equal one additional correct task
findings.evidence: "strong gains in South Asia (+6.6pp) and Oceania (+8.4pp). This region-by-region consistency, not a single number, is the evidence that M-SQE's quality signal captures cultural correctness"; Table 2: "Cultural Skill Use 52" tasks; Fig. 3 extracted region labels: 86.7, 93.3, 91.7, 100.0, 100.0, 91.7
findings.claim: With 52 cultural tasks across six regions (mean 8.7/region), +6.6pp decomposes as 93.3−86.7 = 14/15−13/15 and +8.4pp as 91.7−83.3 = 11/12−10/12 — each exactly one more correct task. For either delta to represent two or more tasks the region would need ≥24 tasks, and two such regions would leave ≤4 tasks for the remaining four. Separately: if the six extracted Fig. 3 labels are one method's per-region rates over a partition of 52 tasks, the minimum feasible denominators (15+15+12+12+1+1 = 56) exceed 52; the label-to-series mapping is ambiguous in text extraction, so this needs author clarification rather than being asserted as an error.
findings.why_it_matters: The social-impact section explicitly offers region-by-region consistency as "the evidence" for cultural-equality impact. One-task-resolution subgroup deltas cannot carry that ethical claim; per-region significance is deferred to Appendix B and unverifiable. The equality framing (abstract: "strong performance across all six culture regions") is overclaimed relative to the sample sizes the main text itself reports.
findings.verifier_note: I recomputed everything and could not refute it. Table 2 gives 52 cultural tasks over six regions (mean 8.67). For a displayed +6.6pp: 93.3-86.7=6.6, and exhaustive check of all n<=52 shows 14/15 vs 13/15 (n=15) is the only realization below n=30 (n=30 needs 28/30 vs 26/30, i.e., 30 of 52 tasks in one region). For +8.4pp: 91.7-83.3=8.4, with 11/12 vs 10/12 (n=12) the only realization below n=24 (22/24 vs 20/24). So 'either delta with >=2 tasks needs >=24 tasks' holds (24 for +8.4, 30 for +6.6), and 52-24-24=4 confirms the extreme-allocation consequence (in fact 24+30=54>52 makes both deltas being 2-task outright infeasible — the finding is understated). Minimum denominators for the six extracted Fig. 3 labels also verify: 86.7 needs n=15, 93.3 needs n=15, 91.7 needs n=12 (twice), 100.0 needs n=1 (twice); 15+15+12+12+1+1=56>52. The finding properly flags the label-to-series attribution as ambiguous per the extraction caveat and requests clarification rather than asserting error. Sec 2's 'strong gains in South Asia (+6.6pp) and Oceania (+8.4pp). This region-by-region consistency ... is the evidence' therefore rests on single-task differences; no rebuttal can make ~9-15-task regions statistically load-bearing at these deltas.

The same unreported group both defined the quality construct M-SQE scores and authored all 411 evaluation queries and, presumably, the cultural gold answers — so the entire benchmark's validity, including its cultural correctness, rests on a team whose composition and language coverage cannot be assessed even in outline from the main text.
findings.verifier_note: Grep confirms no recruitment, compensation, consent, or ethics-review language anywhere in the provided pages (the only 'IRB' hit is the substring in 'the-irb-ehalf', line 135), and the three quotes verify (lines 246-248, 382-385, 257-260). findings.title: Open-source pledge covers skill pools derived from copyrighted sources, with no license or redistribution terms named anywhere in the provided material

Also, the paper's own text suggests transformation rather than verbatim copying ('rendered from', skills 'distilled from domain background documentation', task prompts rewritten to 'copy no text from any pool skill'), which blunts, without resolving, the republication concern.

The quoted deltas all verify exactly: 69.12-65.61=+3.5 vs SkillFlow, 69.12-62.82=+6.3 vs Retrieve-only, 69.12-55.14=+14.0 vs Random.

strengths.title: Near-universal integer consistency of reported percentages with the stated task counts
strengths.why: Every one of the 24 non-Random deterministic cells in Table 3, all 9 cells of Table 4, and all 12 cells of Table 5 is exactly k/n for the stated denominators (e.g., 39.6=105/265, 94.2=49/52, 38.30=36/94, 12.08=32/265). This is strong evidence that the stated task counts are the real denominators of the main tables and results are honestly reported at task granularity; fabricated or carelessly transcribed numbers rarely survive this test 45 times in a row.

strengths.title: Cross-figure and cross-table consistency checks all pass
strengths.location: Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6 (p.7) vs Table 3 (p.6) and Sec. 5.1 (p.4)
strengths.why: Fig. 4's Top-3 value 68.2 equals Table 3's M-SQE BM25 three-domain average (204.5/3=68.17); Fig. 6's main-setting cell (59.6 / 68.2) matches Retrieve-only and M-SQE BM25 averages; Fig. 5's low band around 50-51 matches the Random BM25 three-domain average 50.77 from Table 3; Fig. 5's 1.5%-error star matches the 98.5% router accuracy (6/411); the Prompt-only anchors quoted in Sec. 5.1 (53.2/20.4/46.2) match Table 3 exactly; and SkillFlow-as-selector on the SkillFlow retriever reproduces Retrieve-only(SF) identically (74.5/37.4/90.4) — exactly the idempotence one should see, an unforced internal sanity check that passes.

strengths.title: Setup arithmetic is exact: pool compositions, depth rule, and audit total
strengths.why: All three-layer pool sums are correct (400+550+800=1,750; 1,254+660+385=2,299; 3,384+1,283+618=5,285); the stated depth rule reproduces all three candidate depths (10/20/50); Table 1's per-language estimates sum to 84,680, consistent with the '~84,700' total; and N<=K holds for every reported budget.

strengths.title: Claim wording is calibrated to what the numbers actually show
strengths.why: 'First or tied-first' is verified accurate (two exact ties exist and the wording covers them); 'strictly ahead of both selection anchors in all 9 settings' verifies cell-by-cell; Fig. 6's '+3.5-9.0pp' range matches the six printed deltas; and the routing discussion honestly concedes the router's modest contribution ('routing sharpens the margin, and the two views hold the floor'), which matches the Table 4 arithmetic (Action-only alone is +6.5pp over Retrieve-only).

strengths.title: The router corruption sweep is the one place uncertainty is quantified, and it is done properly
strengths.why: 1,000 seeds per corruption rate with an empirical 95% band is a real stress test with real error bars, run on the component most open to a brittleness objection; the monotone degradation from +8.1pp at 10% to +4.5pp at 90% is internally coherent with the 0%-corruption margin of 8.6pp computable from Table 3.

strengths.title: Arithmetic and cross-figure consistency survives full recomputation
strengths.why: Every number I recomputed checks out: Table 3 row averages (M-SQE 69.1, SkillFlow 65.6, Retrieve-only 62.8, Random 55.1) reproduce the claimed +3.5/+6.3/+14.0pp; every cell is consistent with integer successes over n=94/265/52; the BM25 three-domain averages (68.2 M-SQE, 59.6 Retrieve-only) reappear exactly as Fig 4's Top-3 point and Fig 6's main cell; pool sizes sum correctly (400+550+800=1,750; 1,254+660+385=2,299; 3,384+1,283+618=5,285) and K=10*floor(|S|/1000) reproduces 10/20/50; Table 1 sums to ~84,680 vs the stated ~84,700; the router's 98.5% accuracy matches Fig 5's 1.5%-error star; 'first or tied-first in all 9 settings' and 'strictly ahead of both anchors in all 9' both verify cell-by-cell. No prose-table contradiction found.

strengths.title: The scorer=solver self-consistency confound is directly probed and does not explain the gains
strengths.why: Off-diagonal (scorer != solver) cells exist and remain positive: Gemini scorer -> Qwen3.6-Plus solver +9.0pp; Qwen3.6-Plus scorer -> Gemini solver +6.4pp; +5.0pp on the resynthesized pool. Mixed cells are not systematically smaller than matched cells (+9.0 vs +8.6 same-model), so a scorer preferring skills its own model executes well cannot account for the effect within the two backbones tested. Rebuilding the MT and self-generated layers with a different, stronger LLM (Qwen3.6-Plus) also preserves positive gains (+3.5/+5.0pp), addressing the generation-artifact confound. Caveats: only two scorer models, both strong, and no scorer variation on the resynthesized pool — but the core control is real and passes.

strengths.title: The router-corruption sweep is an honest control that bounds the authors' own component
strengths.why: Randomly flipping router labels on up to 90% of queries, with 1,000 seeds per rate and empirical 95% intervals, both demonstrates robustness (M-SQE stays above Retrieve-only throughout) and transparently quantifies the router's ceiling contribution (~3.6pp between +8.1pp at 10% and +4.5pp at 90% corruption). Publishing a control that limits the importance of one's own framework component is rigorous practice.

strengths.title: Skill-necessity anchor and solver-side anonymization guard against two real confounds
strengths.why: The Prompt-only anchor (53.2/20.4/46.2, all far below M-SQE's results) verifies tasks require skills rather than solver parametric memory — the filter explicitly screens out tasks that 'saturate without any skill'. And the solver receives 'anonymized skill bodies... (provenance labels and source identifiers stripped), without any gold answer or checker metadata' (Sec 4.1), closing the channel where the solver could favor skills by layer or origin.

strengths.title: The headline comparison targets the strongest, most relevant baseline under conditions favorable to it
strengths.why: The +3.5pp headline is computed against SkillFlow — the skill-specific state-of-the-art — whose ranking stage is additionally reused as a selector on top of every retriever, including its own full pipeline (the SF columns), and evaluation spans three retriever families (lexical, dense, skill-specific) so gains are not an artifact of one candidate distribution. Ties are reported as ties ('first or tied-first'), including the two cells where M-SQE only matches a baseline (Tool-Ne 36.2 = SkillFlow; Cultural-Ne 90.4 = mMARCO).

strengths.title: Budget sensitivity covers the deployment-relevant regime with a mechanistically coherent pattern
strengths.why: Testing N in {1,3,5,10} includes the small-context regime real agents occupy, and the margin over Retrieve-only widening as the budget tightens (+3.4pp at Top10 to +9.7pp at Top1) is exactly the signature a genuine selection-quality effect predicts, since larger budgets forgive individual bad picks; the Top-3 point (68.2) is consistent with Table 3.

strengths.title: The central motivational statistic (70.1% adoption, no gain) is verified genuine and correctly attributed
strengths.location: Sec 1 (p2, lines 99-102): "Even in English-only settings, Li et al. (2025) report that agents adopt a relevance-retrieved skill 70.1% of the time with no accompanying performance gain"; re-credited in Sec 4.3 (p3, lines 273-275)
strengths.why: I verified externally (arXiv:2504.06188 and its indexed abstract) that SkillFlow's Terminal-Bench analysis reports exactly this: a 70.1% skill use rate with no performance gain, attributed to the corpus lacking high-quality executable skills. The paper's most load-bearing motivational premise is accurately sourced, correctly quantified, and credited again where the Action view is designed to target it. The same check confirmed the citation's title and four-stage design match the paper's description ('faithfully reimplemented from its four-stage design').

strengths.title: The second motivational premise (curated skills help, self-generated can hurt) is a fair paraphrase of a verified source
strengths.location: Sec 1 (p2, lines 93-95) and Sec 3 (p2, lines 173-176): "Li et al. (2026) show that curated skills raise agent task success while self-generated ones offer little or even negative benefit"
strengths.why: Verified against SkillsBench (arXiv:2602.12670): curated Skills raise average pass rate by 16.2pp with negative deltas on a subset of tasks, and self-generated Skills provide no benefit on average. 'Offer little or even negative benefit' is a faithful, non-inflated paraphrase. Both of the paper's key empirical premises therefore rest on accurately reported prior findings, not on stretched citations.

strengths.title: Honest lineage disclosure and adversarial reuse of the closest competitor
strengths.location: Sec 4.2 (p3, lines 243-245): "These dimensions are inspired by existing multilingual instruction-data quality taxonomy (Liu et al. 2026c), and are further extended to the demands of multilingual agent skills"; Sec 5.3 (p5, lines 475-478, 494-496)
strengths.why: The paper does not claim its quality taxonomy from scratch - it names MIDB as the basis and identifies exactly which dimensions are new (executability, context efficiency, and the Action-view dimensions). It also names SkillFlow as 'the state-of-the-art skill-specific retrieval pipeline', reimplements it both as a retriever and as a post-retrieval selector baseline, and M-SQE is evaluated on top of SkillFlow's own retrieval. Positioning against the strongest prior system by running it, rather than omitting it, is good practice.

strengths.title: The two-family baseline design operationalizes the positioning claim empirically
strengths.location: Sec 3 'Positioning M-SQE' (p3, lines 200-210) mirrored in Sec 5.3 baselines and Table 3 (pp5-6)
strengths.why: The two gaps claimed in Sec 3 (relevance-only skill retrieval; static-only data quality) map one-to-one onto the two baseline families actually run: relevance rerankers (ToolRerank, SkillFlow's ranking stage, mMARCO) and quality scorers (DEITA, M-DaQ, JQL), each repurposed as post-retrieval selectors on identical candidate sets. The positioning is thus tested rather than merely asserted - Table 3 shows both families individually underperform the combination, which is the paper's structural claim. The one family missing is the prompted-LLM reranker (see findings), but what is claimed in Sec 3 is backed by an experiment.

strengths.title: Contribution-bullet arithmetic verifies exactly against Table 3, including the 'first or tied-first in all 9 settings' claim
strengths.location: Sec 1 bullet 1 (p2, lines 119-121) and Sec 5.5 (p6, lines 582-588) vs Table 3 (p6)
strengths.why: Recomputed from Table 3: M-SQE nine-setting average 69.12 vs Retrieve-only 62.83 (+6.29, reported '+6.3pp'), vs Random 55.14 (reported '+14.0pp', actual +13.98), vs SkillFlow 65.61 (+3.51, reported '+3.5pp'). Column-by-column check confirms M-SQE is strictly best in 7 of 9 settings and tied-first in 2 (Tool-Use/Neural 36.2 with SkillFlow; Cultural/Neural 90.4 with mMARCO), exactly matching the hedged wording 'first or tied-first'. The contribution claims are numerically honest to the table (the abstract's per-retriever phrasing is the one exception, filed as a finding).

strengths.title: Two genuinely novel artifacts: the multilingual skill-supply audit and the three-layer mixed-provenance pool design
strengths.location: Table 1 (p1, lines 49-59: en ~79,700 ... sw 0, hi 0 of ~84,700 entries); Sec 5.2 and Table 2 (pp4-5: 'ecological-style 400 + MT 550 + self-generated 800' etc.)
strengths.why: Nothing in the cited literature, and nothing I could find in the adjacent 2025-2026 skill-retrieval literature (SkillRet, SkillRAE, skill-reranking preprints surfaced during verification), audits in-language skill supply across community indexes or constructs evaluation pools that deliberately mix ecological, MT, and self-generated skill provenance per language. These are the paper's clearest first-of-kind contributions, and they give the field a citable empirical fact (zero in-language skill bodies for Swahili and Hindi among ~84,700 entries; protocol deferred to Appendix A, unverifiable from the provided material). My overall verdict for this dimension: the scoring/fusion machinery is standard technique; the rubric content, the setting, the audit, and the pool construction are real contributions - this is a 'standard mechanism, new setting, novel evaluation artifacts, strong execution' paper, which is a legitimate and useful kind of paper, provided the mechanism-level framing is corrected.

strengths.title: Release pledge with a concrete pointer covering exactly the reproduction-critical assets
strengths.why: "We open-source our evaluation set, skill pools, and M-SQE implementation" is backed by footnote 1 ("Code, data and appendices are in Supplementary Material") — a checkable artifact rather than an unpointered promise, and the pledged scope (eval set, pools, implementation) is precisely what a reproducer needs.

strengths.title: Candidate-depth rule and pool arithmetic verified internally consistent
strengths.why: I recomputed K = 10·⌊|S|/1000⌋ against Table 2: 1,750→10, 2,299→20, 5,285→50, all matching the listed depths; the three-layer sums also check out (400+550+800=1,750; 1,254+660+385=2,299; 3,384+1,283+618=5,285). The stated averages also recompute exactly (69.1−65.6=+3.5pp; 69.1−62.8=+6.3pp; 69.1−55.1=+14.0pp).

strengths.title: Scoring math fully specified at formula level in the main text
strengths.why: The complete decision rule is in the reviewed pages: red-line caps (40/80), Cgen = 0.6·Action + 0.4·Theory, the Cfunc lexicographic guard with the explicit Theory≥65 threshold, Ccul as equal per-query z-scores, and Eq. 1's one-hot domain routing — with a perturbation-stability pointer (Appendix C). A reimplementer lacks the prompts but not the algorithm.

strengths.title: Access-dated citations pin the audit snapshot of moving-target community indexes
strengths.why: All three named audit sources carry "Accessed 2026-07-24", giving a point-in-time anchor for star counts and entry counts that would otherwise drift — good hygiene for auditing live repositories.

strengths.title: Solver blinding and skill-necessity anchors stated in the main text
strengths.why: "the downstream solver receives only the query and the anonymized skill bodies ... without any gold answer or checker metadata" states the leakage boundary explicitly, and the Prompt-only anchors (53.2/20.4/46.2) are printed in both Sec 5.1 and Table 3 (they match), making the skill-necessity filter auditable from the main text.

strengths.title: Backbone-dependence partially hedged, including one fully open-weights downstream result
strengths.why: The six-configuration synthesis/scorer/solver grid keeps M-SQE +3.5–9.0pp over Retrieve-only under every swap, and Table 5's fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B gives one result chain that survives any API deprecation — so the qualitative claim does not rest on a single proprietary model even though the exact headline numbers do.

strengths.title: Double-anonymity check passed
strengths.why: Anonymous byline, no self-identifying URLs, acknowledgments, or first-person references to prior work. The heavily-used related papers with overlapping author lists (MIDB, M-DaQ, MADE, GaoYao) are cited strictly in third person, which standard double-anonymous policy explicitly permits; I found no plausible anonymity violation.
